newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Crackdown talk sends Shenzhen B index to end lower.
newsitem.headline: Crackdown talk sends Shenzhen B index to end lower.

text.p: Shenzhen B shares closed sharply lower on Tuesday amid talk of further government crackdown measures on trading misconduct, traders said.

The foreign currency B share index sagged 3.66 points or 2.43 percent to end at 147.11 on turnover of HK$108.9 million against Friday's HK$87 million. The B share market was closed on Monday for a public holiday in neighbouring Hong Kong.
The domestic currency A share index plunged 19.21 points or 4.31 percent to 426.45 on turnover of 6.0 billion yuan compared with Monday's 7.2 billion yuan.
"Talk of an imminent government announcement on punishing misbehaving brokerages is keeping buyers off the markets," a trader at China Guotai Securities said.
In May, the markets reacted sharply to rumours that Beijing would ban four of China's biggest brokerages from trading on their own accounts and would fine them for alleged trading misconduct.
"We are all quite certain the clampdown will take place, it's just a matter of when the government chooses to announce it," an analyst at China Securities said.
Analysts said they expected the A share market to fall more than 15 percent in the next several weeks, but foresaw a flatter B index slide.
"Some investors who are wary about the A share market are turning to the cheaper and less risky B shares," the China Securities analyst said.
The B share market is technically restricted to foreign investors but mainland Chinese trade on the market through various channels.
On the B share market, the biggest loser was SEZ Real Estate and Properties Group Co Ltd which dived HK$0.26 or 7.54 percent to HK$3.19.
Beijing Orient Electronics Group Co made its debut on Tuesday, ending at HK$3.91 compared with an offer price of HK$3.08.
Weak market sentiment resulting from recent government measures aimed at squeezing bank funds out of the stock markets capped the newcomer's gains, traders said.
Beijing last week ordered all state banks to unwind their stock market positions within 10 sessions to reduce the flow of "hot money", or speculative funds, into the markets.
Banks were also told to cease trading on the treasury debt repurchase market, through which they had channelled large amounts of funds into the equity markets.
The ban followed recent moves to bar state and listed firms from speculative stock trading.
The worst A share performer was Jinxing Development, which closed at its 10 percent limit-down level at 9.68 yuan.
